experiment.title: Saturation Genome Editing of SBDS
experiment.shortDescription: We used saturation genome editing to measure the effect of 2,675 SBDS SNVs and 640 3-base pair deletions on SBDS-dependent HAP1 cell survival.
experiment.abstractText: Genetic variants in the SBDS gene are associated with the rare inherited disease Shwachman-Diamond Syndrome (SDS). Many variants that cause rare diseases like SDS are single nucleotide variants (SNVs) with uncertain pathogenicity. Such variants of uncertain significance (VUS) are problematic in the clinic because they cannot inform diagnoses and interventions. Functional data can provide evidence for classifying variants as pathogenic or benign. Saturation Genome Editing (SGE) was applied to assess the functional impact of all possible missense variants and trinucleotide deletions of SBDS to generate evidence on their pathogenicity to improve information available to clinicians and patients. SGE on all 5 exons of SBDS generated a total of 3,315 variant scores. We identify 93.3% of stop gain variants (111 of 119) and 87.5% of splice site variants (63 of 72) as functionally abnormal. Of 1,580 missense variants, 146 (9.24%) score as loss-of-function, 1,423 (90.1%) as functionally normal, and 11 (0.70%) as indeterminate. SGE scores are highly concordant with ClinVar annotations, where 79.2% of assayed clinically known pathogenic variants (19 of 24) correctly score as functionally abnormal and all 91 known benign variants correctly score as functionally normal. Taken together, these suggest that SGE is an effective assay for SBDS.
experiment.methodText: Functional scores for 2,675 SNVs and 640 3-bp deletions were calculated by applying a negative binomial regression model to variant counts across all sampled time points and replicates. Variants near 0 represent no change, loss of function variants have progressively more negative scores
